o: Among towers whose Manhattan distance to center is at most radius, return the coordinates of the one with the highest quality factor, breaking ties by lexicographically smaller (x, y); return [-1,-1] if none is reachable. In example 1 all three towers are reachable and quality 9 wins at [3,1]; in example 2 the far tower is out of range and the tie between qualities 4 goes to [1,3]; in example 3 nothing is reachable. A single linear scan with a tuple comparison (-quality, x, y) solves it in O(n).
k: Reachability is Manhattan distance <= radius - a cheap per-tower check.
Best tower = lexicographic minimum of the tuple (-q, x, y) over reachable towers.
No sorting or data structures are needed; one pass suffices.

a.n: Approach 1: Linear scan with tuple comparison
a.i: Track the best (-quality, x, y) triple seen; a tower replaces it only if its triple is smaller, which encodes 'higher quality first, then smaller x, then smaller y' exactly.
s: For each tower, if Manhattan distance <= radius, compare (-q, x, y) with best and keep the smaller.
Return best's coordinates, or [-1,-1] if best stayed null.
a.t: O(n) - one comparison pass over the towers

w: This is an exercise in careful tie-breaking: encode it once as a tuple and the code writes itself. Pitfalls: using Euclidean instead of Manhattan distance, breaking ties by array order instead of lexicographic coordinates, and forgetting the unreachable [-1,-1] case. Follow-up: k nearest towers, or quality decaying with distance.
